newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Strong Irish Exchequer data seen bullish for bonds.
newsitem.headline: Strong Irish Exchequer data seen bullish for bonds.

text.p: Ireland's Exchequer surprised financial markets on Tuesday by announcing a much stronger-than-expected Exchequer surplus at end-July which economists said was bullish for bonds.

"It just goes to show the strength of the consumer economy and it will be very positive for the bond market as the government will have very little funding needs," AIB Capital Markets economist Pat O'Sullivan told Reuters.

Ireland's Finance Ministry said end-July Exchequer returns showed a surplus of 929 million Irish pounds versus an Exchequer surplus of 721 million punts at end-June and against forecasts of between 570 to 600 million punts surplus.
"For bonds there is a marked lack of supply," Riada economist Dan McLaughlin said. "At the moment there is one auction a month and there hasn't been a tap in the market since April."
"So if there is any demand in the market, there is very little supply to meet it and bonds can be pushed ahead quite a lot."

Economists said the strong Exchequer figure once again underlined the exceptional buoyancy of the Irish economy and some said they were revising forecasts for end-year Exchequer funding needs to show a small deficit, at worst, but most expected the government's coffers to be in surplus.
"Revenue continues to be strong. It was up 15.5 percent and the government's projection was for something less than half of that," NCB stockbrokers economist Eunan King said.
Tuesday's data showed the Exchequer benefiting from strong tax revenue with total tax receipts up at 8.42 billion Irish pounds at end-July compared with 7.29 billion pounds at end-July 1996.
King said as data for seven months was so strong it looked like the Exchequer was heading for a zero borrowing requirement or perhaps for a surplus for the year.
The government announced an Exchequer Borrowing target for 1997 of 637 million punts at its annual budget at the beginning of the year.
"I would be putting in a surplus of about 200 million punts for the year that should be easily attainable. To go into deficit would be ridiculous," AIB's O'Sullivan said.
"The figure is certainly better-than-expected," Riada's McLaughlin said. "We have seen a very strong acceleration on the revenue side and spending is running beneath target."
McLaughlin said he was going for a zero funding requirement at the end of the year.
Bank of Ireland economist Jim Power took a more cautious attitude forecasting a borrowing requirement in the region of 300 million punts for 1997.

"They were very strong numbers and will put the minister in a very comfortable position funding-wise," Jim Power said. "I am forecasting an annual funding requirement of less than 300 million punts based on these numbers."
